extracted.intended_audience: readers and researchers interested in the history of mathematics, historians of science, and students of Thomas Hariot
extracted.subtask_description: Excerpt from a historical biography recounting Thomas Hariot's life, mathematical works (especially his Artis Analyticae Praxis), the publication history, manuscript disposition, and controversies over priority and editorial duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Posthumous manuscript stewardship (as specified in Hariot's will)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hariot's will prescribes specific procedures and persons for managing his mathematical and other writings after his death.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Item in the will: Nathaniel Torporley is appointed 'first to be Overseer of my Mathematical Writings to be received of my Executors to peruse and order and to separate the Chiefe of them from my waste papers, to the end that after hee doth vnderstand them hee may make use in penning such doctrine that belongs vnto them for publique vses as it shall be thought Convenient by my Executors and him selfe.' If any notation or writings are not understood by him he is to 'conferre with Mr Warner or Mr Hughes ... or ... John Protheroe ... or Thomas Alesbury' and, after use, the papers are to be delivered to executors, put into a trunk with a lock and key, and placed in the Earl of Northumberland's library with the key delivered to his Lordship. Executors and Torporley may later request temporary return of papers for use, after which they should be restored to the trunk. (Full procedural text quoted/paraphrased from pages 165–167.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial responsibilities for preparing unfinished scientific papers
rubrics_metrics.description: When papers are not left ready for publication, an editor/overseer must peruse, arrange, weed out waste papers, master the material, and prepare doctrine for public use under the supervision of executors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As described: 'No papers were left ready for publication. It must have required great study and labor to master them sufficiently to pen for public use such doctrine or science as belonged to them.' Torporley was expected to 'peruse and order and to separate the Chiefe of them from my waste papers' and then to 'pen' such doctrine for public use subject to the executors' judgment. If notation was unclear he was to consult named knowledgeable persons. The process includes thorough study, arrangement, possible consultation, and preparation for publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cataloguing and physical management of manuscript collections
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuscript collections should be catalogued, arranged in packets, numbered, described, and preserved appropriately to prevent loss and enable future research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from the text: collections arranged 'in packets by Professor Rigaud'; descriptions include 'A black leather box containing several hundred leaves of figures and calculations'; lists of contents (e.g., Spots on the Sun, Comets of 1607 and 1618, The Moon, Jupiter's Satellites, Projectiles, Centre of Gravity, Algebra, etc.). Manuscripts preserved in Solander cases, catalogued as Additional 6782-6789 in the British Museum; a recommendation implicit in the narrative is to catalog, number, bind, and describe the contents to avoid loss (contrast with scattered collections and possible losses in the fire of London).

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for sequencing publication of an author's works
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors may choose to publish a preliminary or introductory treatise first if it conveniently serves as preparation for the author's remaining works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted explanatory note 'To Students of Mathematics': '... this preliminary treatise, besides its own inestimable utility, might suitably serve as a necessary preparation or introduction to the study of Harriot's remaining works, the publication of which is now under serious consideration.' Thus one editorial criterion is pedagogical utility: publish the work that best prepares readers for the rest of the corpus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for attributing originality and assessing plagiarism in the history of mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: Determinations of priority and plagiarism should consider dates of invention versus dates of publication, the principal subject/domain of the work (e.g., geometry vs algebra), and whether the alleged borrowing is of incidental tools/notation or of the central contribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narrative points: Wallis accused Descartes of taking algebraic methods from Hariot, noting similar notation and techniques; the counterargument emphasized that Hariot's method predated Descartes and that Descartes' main contribution was in geometry (not algebra), so use of algebraic notation as an 'incidental aid' does not constitute plagiarism of the central work. Also the text stresses the importance of when a method was in practical use (among disciples) vs its first printed appearance; 'priority' disputes require scrutiny of invention date, circulation among pupils, and publication date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid judging a mathematician solely by a single printed work
rubrics_metrics.description: A scholar's reputation should be assessed on the totality of their discoveries, manuscripts, and contributions rather than hinging chiefly upon one printed book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text criticizes the misconception that Hariot's reputation 'has been permitted to hinge chiefly upon' his Algebra (Praxis), noting that this is 'very much to his disadvantage' because many of his discoveries remained unpublished or in manuscripts; 'one is forced, therefore, to the conclusion that by 1600... Hariot had completed his method in Algebra' and had many other 'inventions' that affect a fair estimate of his standing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities that make a mathematical treatise useful to students
rubrics_metrics.description: A treatise that serves students well typically is composed of varied specimens of reasoning, written in a clear logical style, and can act as a preparatory introduction to more advanced works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the editors' preface describing Harriot's Praxis: the treatise 'consists entirely of varied specimens of beautiful reasoning' and is written 'in the same, hitherto unusual, logical style'—these features justify publishing it first 'that this preliminary treatise... might suitably serve as a necessary preparation or introduction to the study of Harriot's remaining works.'
